# Diagnosing and Resolving Ignition Key Lockouts in 2007 Ford Fusion

When a key remains physically locked inside the ignition of a 2007 Ford Fusion, even with the transmission in Park, the issue is almost exclusively mechanical or related to the electrical interlock system rather than a software glitch. Unlike modern vehicles where firmware updates might resolve access control logic, this era of automotive engineering relies on physical tumblers and dedicated safety switches. Understanding the architecture of this specific failure mode requires looking at how the ignition switch communicates with the transmission range sensor.

The core mechanism preventing the key from turning back to the "Off" position is typically the Neutral Safety Switch (or Transmission Range Sensor). This component ensures the vehicle cannot be started unless it is in Park or Neutral and prevents the key from removing while the car is in gear. In a 2007 Fusion, if the ignition switch has not received the correct signal confirming the car is in Park, it mechanically locks the key cylinder. It is crucial to distinguish between the electrical circuit and the physical actuator; the problem usually lies in the mechanical linkage or the sensor's adjustment, not the electronic control module itself.

Before attempting invasive disassembly, verify the transmission range sensor alignment. The issue often stems from the cable connecting the shift lever to the transmission being slightly out of calibration. If the sensor does not accurately detect the "Park" position, the ignition remains locked. The resolution involves accessing the sensor near the firewall or under the dash, depending on the specific trim level. You will need to loosen the mounting bracket screws and manually adjust the cable tension until the vehicle is securely in Park and the key turns freely. Once adjusted, tighten the bracket but leave the adjustment screw slightly loose initially to allow for minor thermal expansion of the transmission casing over time.

If adjustment fails, inspect the ignition switch assembly itself. Over 15 years of usage, the internal contacts or the detent spring within the switch can degrade. When this happens, the switch may fail to return to the "Off" electrical state even if the mechanical tumblers are turned. In this scenario, replacing the entire ignition lock cylinder and switch assembly is often more cost-effective than sourcing individual components, as these are rarely sold separately for older model years. Removal requires disconnecting the battery negative terminal first to prevent any accidental short circuits while working near the steering column wiring harness.

There is a secondary possibility involving the shift interlock solenoid. While this usually prevents shifting out of Park without pressing the brake pedal, in some Fusion configurations, a failure here can create a feedback loop that confuses the ignition logic. Check if the brake light switch is functioning correctly, as many modern Fords require a valid "brake applied" signal to allow the shift interlock to disengage, which in turn might be required for the ignition to unlock fully in certain software interpretations of the safety protocol.

Finally, consider the key itself. If the tumblers inside the ignition cylinder are worn down or if the key blade is damaged, it may not engage the pins deep enough to allow the switch to return to the neutral position. Try a spare key immediately; if the spare works smoothly, the issue is purely within the lock cylinder's internal mechanism. If neither adjustment nor a spare key resolves the issue, professional replacement of the ignition assembly is the only viable path forward. Avoid forcing the key with excessive torque, as this can snap the plastic housing around the switch, turning a repairable sensor issue into a full steering column teardown.
